unit.title: Sound
unit.blurb: How vibrations make sound, why sound needs a medium, reading waveforms for amplitude, wavelength and frequency, loudness and pitch, and how sound waves interfere.

O1.t: Describe how vibrating objects produce sound as compressions and rarefactions that travel through a medium.

O2.t: Identify crest, trough, amplitude and wavelength on a waveform and draw waveforms.

O3.t: Relate amplitude to loudness and frequency to pitch.

O4.t: Describe constructive and destructive interference of sound waves and their uses.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 11: Sound.
Close your eyes and listen.
A car engine, a bird singing, people talking: some sounds are loud,
some soft, some high, some low.
Where do sounds come from, and how do they reach your ears?
All sounds come from vibrating, or oscillating, objects.
A plucked guitar string, a drum membrane, the reed of a saxophone,
your vocal cords and a speaker cone all vibrate.
A speaker cone moving forward squeezes air particles together: a compression.
Moving back, it spreads them apart: a rarefaction.
These travel outwards as a sound wave,
passing energy from particle to particle to your ear.
Sound needs a medium to travel through.
The closer the particles, the faster sound travels: fastest in solids, then liquids,
then gases. In a vacuum there are no particles, so sound can't travel at all.
Space is silent!
An electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar.
A pump slowly removes the air from the jar.
Predict: what will happen to the sound we hear?
Pause and decide.
Watch. As the air is pumped out, the ringing gets quieter and quieter.
With almost all the air removed, we can hardly hear anything,
although we can still see the hammer hitting the bell.
Explain what you saw.
The bell still vibrates,
but sound needs particles to carry the vibrations
to the glass and then to our ears.
As the air is removed,
there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations, so the sound fades.
In a vacuum, sound cannot travel at all.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
The speed of sound depends on the material it travels through.
These are typical values.
In air at 20 degrees Celsius,
sound travels at about 343 metres per second.
In water it is about 1480, and in steel nearly 6000.
Pause and decide: why is sound fastest in steel and slowest in air?

captions: An oscilloscope displays sound as a waveform.
The highest point is the crest, the lowest the trough.
The amplitude is the height from the equilibrium line to a crest,
and the wavelength is the length of one cycle.
To draw a waveform graph, label the axes and choose even scales.
Mark the amplitude above and below the equilibrium line, mark one cycle's time,
then draw a smooth curve through the crests and troughs.
The bigger the amplitude, the more energy a sound carries,
and the louder it sounds.
Loudness is measured on the decibel scale,
from rustling leaves to a jet taking off.
Too much noise can cause stress and hearing loss.
Frequency is the number of waves per second, measured in hertz.
Higher frequency means higher pitch: a violin sounds high, a bass guitar low.
Humans hear from about 20 to 20 thousand hertz.
US health agencies publish typical sound levels for everyday noises, measured in decibels.
A whisper is about 30 decibels and normal conversation about 60.
A lawnmower reaches about 90, a loud concert about 105,
an emergency siren about 120, and a jet taking off about 140.
Pause and decide: which of these could damage your
hearing if you listened for a long time?

captions: When sound waves meet, they interfere.
If they're in phase, crests line up with crests,
and their amplitudes add together, making a louder sound.
This is constructive interference, used in some hearing aids.
If they're out of phase, crests meet troughs and cancel out: destructive interference.
Noise-cancelling headphones record outside noise, reverse it,
and play it back to cancel the noise.
Now it is your turn to shine!

Question 1: How is sound produced?
Pause the video now.
Answer: By vibrating objects.
Question 2: Why can't sound travel through space?
Pause the video now.
Answer: There are no particles to carry it: it's a vacuum.
Question 3: What property of a wave decides how loud it is?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Its amplitude.
Question 4: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Destructive interference: out-of-phase sound cancels noise.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A student walks in front of two speakers playing the same note and hears it get loud, quiet, loud. Explain.

rubric.pt: waves from both speakers overlap / interfere
loud: in phase, constructive
quiet: out of phase, destructive

adv.model: The waves from the two speakers overlap and interfere. Where they arrive in phase, constructive interference makes it loud; where they arrive out of phase, destructive interference makes it quiet.
